scenario.topic: Choose the sprint cadence for a software development team

options.name: One-Week Sprint Cadence
options.upside: Enables rapid feedback and frequent delivery.
options.concern: High planning overhead may reduce development time.

options.name: Two-Week Sprint Cadence
options.upside: Balances delivery speed with manageable planning effort.
options.concern: Less frequent releases may delay stakeholder feedback.

options.name: Three-Week Sprint Cadence
options.upside: Reduces planning overhead and allows more development time.
options.concern: Longer feedback cycles may slow adaptation to changes.

options.name: Four-Week Sprint Cadence
options.concern: Infrequent releases can delay detection of issues.

shared_context: The team must select a sprint cadence that balances delivery frequency and planning overhead. The sprint length should accommodate four developers and support consistent progress tracking and stakeholder feedback.

personas.name: Maya
personas.background: Maya is a product owner focused on balancing delivery speed with team efficiency.
personas.private_goal: Ensure the team maintains a steady delivery pace without excessive planning overhead.

A.reason_for: Enables rapid feedback and frequent delivery, which can help catch issues early.
A.reason_against: High planning overhead may reduce valuable development time.

B.reason_for: Balances delivery speed with manageable planning effort, fitting the team size well.

C.reason_for: Reduces planning overhead and allows more uninterrupted development time.
C.reason_against: Longer feedback cycles may slow adaptation to changes.

D.reason_against: Infrequent releases can delay detection of issues and stakeholder feedback.

personas.name: Liam
personas.background: Liam is a senior developer who values a sustainable pace and clear communication.
personas.private_goal: Keep planning overhead low while maintaining frequent enough releases for feedback.

A.reason_for: Frequent releases enable rapid feedback and continuous improvement.
A.reason_against: Too many planning meetings can interrupt development flow.

B.reason_for: Offers a good balance between delivery frequency and planning effort.

C.reason_for: Fewer planning meetings mean more development time.
C.reason_against: Longer sprints might delay stakeholder feedback and slow adaptation.

D.reason_against: Infrequent releases risk late detection of issues.

personas.name: Zoe
personas.background: Zoe is a quality assurance engineer who prioritizes thorough testing and stability.
personas.private_goal: Minimize disruptions and maximize development time to ensure quality.

A.reason_for: Rapid feedback can help catch issues early.
A.reason_against: High planning overhead and frequent context switching reduce focus on quality.

B.reason_for: Balances delivery and planning, allowing reasonable testing cycles.
B.reason_against: Still may feel rushed for thorough quality assurance.

C.reason_for: More development time allows for deeper testing and stability.
C.reason_against: Longer feedback cycles might delay issue detection.

D.reason_for: Maximizes uninterrupted development and testing periods, improving quality.

personas.name: Eli
personas.background: Eli is a UX designer who values quick iterations and frequent user feedback.
personas.private_goal: Ensure the team delivers often enough to gather user insights regularly.

A.reason_for: Enables rapid feedback and frequent delivery, ideal for quick UX iterations.

B.reason_for: Balances delivery frequency with planning effort, still supporting regular feedback.
B.reason_against: Less frequent releases may slow down user insight gathering.

C.reason_for: Reduces planning overhead, allowing more focus on design implementation.
C.reason_against: Longer sprints delay feedback cycles, impacting UX responsiveness.

D.reason_against: Infrequent releases delay user feedback, which is critical for UX.
